citation.title: Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment

standing_assumptions:
[Population and design: pp. 1914–1915 (PDF pp. 3–4)] Formally, suppose we have a finite population $U$ of units indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$ on which a randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, M\}$ specifies which of $M$ possible treatment values that unit $i$ receives. An experimental design contains a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ from the $M^N$ different possibilities with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by a given experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$ so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Our analysis below focuses on the case where the design is known in the following sense: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ for all $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ is known. [Exposure mapping: p. 1915 (PDF p. 4)] We define an exposure mapping as a function that maps an assignment vector and unit-specific traits to an exposure value: $f : \Omega 	imes \Theta 	o \Delta$, where $	heta_i \in \Theta$ quantifies relevant traits of unit $i$. [Exposures and exposure probabilities: p. 1916 (PDF p. 5)] Define the exposure that unit $i$ receives as $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z}, 	heta_i)$, a random variable with support $\Delta_i \subseteq \Delta$ and for which $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. Note that because $|\Delta| \le |\Omega| 	imes N$, $\Delta$ is a finite set of $K \le |\Omega| 	imes N$ values, such that $\Delta = \{d_1, \ldots, d_K\}$. Then for each unit, $i$, we have a vector of probabilities, $(\pi_i(d_1), \ldots, \pi_i(d_K))' =  oldsymbol{\pi}_i$. [...] We have $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)$. [...] we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$ as the probability of the joint event that both units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposure $d_k$, and we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ as the probability of the joint event that units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposures $d_k$ and $d_l$, respectively. [Probability matrices: p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ is an $N 	imes N$ symmetric matrix with individual exposure probabilities, the $\pi_i(d_k)$'s, on the diagonal and joint exposure probabilities, the $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$'s, on the off-diagonals. The nonsymmetric $N 	imes N$ matrix $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$, with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$, yields all joint probabilities across exposure conditions $k$ and $l$. The zeroes on the diagonal are due to the fact that a unit cannot be subject to multiple exposure conditions at once. [Positivity: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] Suppose all units have nonzero probabilities of being subject to each of the $K$ exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and $k$. [Potential outcomes: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] In the most general terms, each $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ can generate a potential outcome for unit $i$. We label the randomization potential outcome of unit $i$ associated with $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$. These randomization potential outcomes are fixed for all units in the population and do not depend on the value of randomized treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$. CONDITION 1 (Properly specified exposure mapping). For all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', 	heta_i)$, $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Given Condition 1, each unit $i$ has $|\Delta| = K$ potential outcomes, which we can write in terms of the exposure conditions as $(y_i(d_1), \ldots, y_i(d_K))$, where $y_i(d_k) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, and $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k$. Let $Y_i$ be the observed outcome for unit $i$. CONDITION 2 (Consistent potential outcomes). $Y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) y_i(d_k)$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. [p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] Throughout, unless otherwise noted, we will be assuming Conditions 1 and 2. [Estimands: p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] We seek estimates for all $k$ of $\mu(d_k) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) =  rac{1}{N} y^T(d_k)$, where $y^T(d_k)$ is the total of the potential outcomes under $d_k$. This allows us to define an average causal effect of being in exposure condition $d_k$ as compared to being in condition $d_l$ as $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) -  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_l)$. [Estimators: pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] (1) $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}$. $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) = (1/N)\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) = (1/N^2)\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. (3) $\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_l) =  rac{1}{N}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$, which is an estimator of $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]$, the average unit-level causal effect of exposure $k$ versus exposure $l$. [Exact probabilities: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9)] from here on our analysis assumes that we are working with $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ and $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$ [the exact exposure probabilities; the simulated probabilities $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ enter only Propositions 3.1 and 4.1]. [Variance and covariance estimators of Section 5, used by several targets: pp. 1921–1924 (PDF pp. 10–13)] Given $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, the Horvitz–Thompson estimator for $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is (7) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i \in U} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)[1 - \pi_i(d_k)] \left[ rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}ight]^2 + \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) 	imes  rac{\pi_{ij}(d_k) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_k)}$. [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] (This notation requires that we define $0/0 = 0$.) [p. 1922] $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_k)}ight]$, noting that $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = 0$ if $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$. [p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] For the case where $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$, we propose the Horvitz–Thompson-type estimator for the covariance (8) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_l) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] a more general estimator for the covariance (10) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924] we obtain a conservative variance estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l))$ as (11) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] =  rac{1}{N^2}\{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_l) - 2\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]\}$. [Asymptotic framework and the conditions of Section 6. These are not standing assumptions: they are transcribed here once because several targets invoke them, and a target carries one of them only where its statement names it.] [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] Consider a sequence of nested populations indexed by size $N$, $(U_N)$. To define a notion of asymptotic growth, we let $N$ tend to infinity, allowing for the experimental design to be reapplied anew to each $U_N$, subject to the conditions defined below. [p. 1925 (PDF p. 14)] CONDITION 3 (Boundedness of potential outcomes and exposure probabilities). Potential outcomes and exposure probabilities are bounded so that, for all values $i$ and $d_k$, $|y_i(d_k)| \le c_1 < \infty$ and $|1/\pi_i(d_k)| \le c_2 < \infty$. [p. 1925] Define a pairwise dependency indicator $g_{ij}$ such that if $g_{ij} = 0$, then $D_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_j$, else let $g_{ij} = 1$. CONDITION 4 (Restrictions on pairwise dependence). $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = o(N^2)$. [p. 1925, as printed] Define a binary dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ over all pairs $(i, j) \in \{1, 2, \ldots, N\} 	imes \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$, where $h_{ij}$ satisfies the following: for any pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2 \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ such that there exists no pair $(i, j)$ with $h_{ij} = 1$ and either (i) $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j 
otin \Gamma_2$, (ii) $j \in \Gamma_1$ and $i 
otin \Gamma_2$, (iii) $i 
otin \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, or (iv) $j 
otin \Gamma_1$ and $i \in \Gamma_2$, $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_1\}$ and $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_2\}$ are independent. CONDITION 5 (Local dependence). There exists a finite constant $m$ such that, for all $U_N$, $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$. [p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] CONDITION 6 (Nonzero limiting variance.). $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} c$, where $c > 0$. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are taken over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$ with weights $p_{\mathbf{z}}$; the population, the traits $	heta_i$, the exposure mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. $U \setminus i$ means $U \setminus \{i\}$. Each unit receives exactly one exposure, so $\sum_{k} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) = 1$, $\pi_{ii}(d_k) = \pi_i(d_k)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d_k, d_l) = 0$ for $d_k 
e d_l$. Wherever two exposures $d_k$, $d_l$ appear together (Proposition 4.2, expressions (6) and (8)–(11), Section 6) they are distinct. The left side of Condition 6 is a deterministic sequence, so the printed $\xrightarrow{p}$ is ordinary convergence. Appendix A.6 (p. 1942) writes $c_3$ for a bound on $|y_i(d_k)|/\pi_i(d_k)$, which Condition 3 gives with $c_3 = c_1c_2$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1926 (PDF p. 15); proof in Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] PROPOSITION 6.2. Given Conditions 3, 5, and 6, Wald-type intervals constructed as $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}$ will tend to cover $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ at least $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ of the time for large $N$. [Proof step refuted: Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)] Denote $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ as the sum of the elements in $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ that incorporate observations $i$ and $j$. Note that all $a_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$ are bounded above by some finite constant by Condition 3 [...] Thus, $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] = O(N^{-2} \times N) = O(N^{-1})$. [Counterexample, from the validator] For even $N \ge 4$ put $n = N/2$, $\epsilon_N = N^{-2}$, $q_N = 1/2 - \epsilon_N$ and $t_N = 1 - 2\epsilon_N = 2q_N$. Let $U_N = \{1, \ldots, N\}$, with pairs $(2r - 1, 2r)$, $1 \le r \le n$. Treatment is binary, $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. The pairs are randomized independently, and within every pair $(a, b)$ $\Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (0, 0)\} = \Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (1, 1)\} = \epsilon_N$ and $\Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (0, 1)\} = \Pr\{(Z_a, Z_b) = (1, 0)\} = q_N$; the probability of a complete assignment is the product of its pair probabilities. Exposure is own assignment, $D_i = Z_i$, with $d_k = 1$ and $d_l = 0$. The potential outcomes are $y_{2r-1}(1) = y_{2r-1}(0) = 1$ and $y_{2r}(1) = y_{2r}(0) = -1$, so $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$ and $\tau(d_k, d_l) = 0$. The populations are nested, outcomes of existing units never change, and the design is reapplied at each $N$, as p. 1924 allows. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] Conditions 1 and 2 hold. $\pi_i(1) = \pi_i(0) = 1/2$ for every unit and $|y_i(d)| = 1$, so Condition 3 holds with $c_1 = 1$, $c_2 = 2$. For distinct units $a, b$ in the same pair, $\pi_{ab}(1) = \pi_{ab}(0) = \epsilon_N$ and $\pi_{ab}(1, 0) = \pi_{ab}(0, 1) = q_N$; for units in different pairs every joint exposure probability equals $1/4$; so every joint exposure probability of two distinct units is positive. With $h_{ij} = 1$ when $i$ and $j$ are in the same pair (including $i = j$) and $h_{ij} = 0$ otherwise, the exposure vectors of any two disjoint sets of units with no $h$-edge between them are independent, and $\sum_j h_{ij} = 2$: Condition 5 holds with $m = 2$ as a genuine dependency graph (the definition corrected as in P013-T6), and also as printed. $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 8t_N/N$, so $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 8(1 - 2/N^2) \to 8$: Condition 6 holds with $c = 8$. (b) [The printed estimator.] Writing $\widehat{V}_N$ for expression (11), $N^2\widehat{V}_N = \sum_{r=1}^{n} R_r$, where for the pair $(a, b) = (2r - 1, 2r)$, $R_r = 2/\epsilon_N$ if $Z_a = Z_b$ and $R_r = 16 - 4/t_N$ if $Z_a \ne Z_b$. $\mathrm{E}[R_r] = 16t_N$, so $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N] = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ exactly, and every value of $\widehat{V}_N$ is positive. (c) [The variance estimator does not concentrate at or above the true variance.] Let $A_N$ be the event that every pair is split ($Z_a \ne Z_b$ in every pair). Then $\Pr(A_N) = t_N^{N/2}$, $\Pr(A_N^c) \le n \cdot 2\epsilon_N = 1/N$, and on $A_N$, $N\widehat{V}_N = 8 - 2/t_N$. Hence $N\widehat{V}_N \xrightarrow{p} 6$ while $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \to 8$, and $\widehat{V}_N/\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} 3/4$. (d) [The bound of Appendix A.7 fails.] $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = \frac{4(N-2)^4(N+2)^4}{N^5(N^2-2)}$, which is asymptotic to $4N$ and tends to infinity; it is not $O(N^{-1})$. (e) [Coverage is below nominal in the limit.] $\sqrt{N}\,\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, 8)$, and for every $0 < \alpha < 1$ $\lim_{N \to \infty} \Pr\{|\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}\} = 2\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{3/4}) - 1 < 1 - \alpha$ (limit along even $N$). For $\alpha = 0.05$ the limit is $0.9103748944\ldots$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. In this instance $M = 2$ with treatment values written $0, 1$, $K = 2$, $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = z_i$, and $\Omega$ is all of $\{0, 1\}^N$. $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution and $\Phi$ its distribution function. The paper does not define $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ without a hat; the coverage target is $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-E012, P013-T9).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each even $N \ge 4$: the marginal and joint exposure probabilities in (a); the pair score $T_r = 4(Z_a - Z_b)$ with $\Pr(T_r = 0) = 2\epsilon_N$, $\Pr(T_r = 4) = \Pr(T_r = -4) = q_N$, $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = N^{-1}\sum_r T_r$ and $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] = 16nt_N/N^2 = 8t_N/N$; the reduction of (7), (10), (11) to $N^2\widehat{V}_N = \sum_r R_r$ in (b) (the $\widehat{A_2}$ terms vanish, and the only zero joint probabilities in (10) are those with $i = j$); $\mathrm{E}[R_r] = (2\epsilon_N)(2/\epsilon_N) + t_N(16 - 4/t_N) = 16t_N$; $\mathrm{E}[R_r^2] = 8/\epsilon_N + t_N(16 - 4/t_N)^2$; $\Pr(A_N) = t_N^{N/2}$ and $\Pr(A_N^c) \le 1/N$; the closed form for $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N)$ in (d). Exact values at $N = 6$ from the validator's enumeration of all 64 assignments: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}_6] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_6) = \mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_6] = 34/27$, $\Pr(A_6) = 4913/5832$, $6\widehat{V}_6 = 100/17$ on $A_6$, $6\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_6) = 68/9$, $\mathrm{Var}(6\widehat{V}_6) = 65536/4131$. The limit statements in (c)–(e) then use $\Pr(A_N^c) \to 0$, the characteristic function $[2\epsilon_N + t_N\cos(4u/\sqrt{N})]^{N/2} \to \exp(-4u^2)$ of $\sqrt{N}\,\widehat{\tau}_N$, and Slutsky's theorem.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E001 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json; lowered from Major after a settled doubt, validate/P013-E001/doubt/doubt.json, found that the added condition is a mild regularity condition which the paper's own designs satisfy), so this target and P013-T2 have priority 2. The second validator's witness (validate/P013-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md) is the same family with $\epsilon_n = 1/(4n^3)$. For a sequence at every integer $N$ the validator adds, at odd $N$, one independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ unit with both potential outcomes equal to 1; failure along even $N$ already refutes the proposition. Proposition 5.6 holds in the witness, with equality. Not established: that coverage can tend to zero, or that any interval reported in the paper undercovers.

canonical_claim.location: p. 1926 (PDF p. 15); proof in Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected Proposition 6.2. Changes from the printed statement: (1) one hypothesis, (L) below, is added; (2) the dependency indicator of Condition 5 is the corrected one of P013-T6; (3) the coverage target is $\tau(d_k, d_l)$, in place of the undefined $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-T9); (4) the conclusion is a lower limit of the coverage probability, with no claim that the variance ratio or the studentized statistic converges (P013-T8).] [Setting] A sequence of nested finite populations $U_N$, $N \to \infty$. For each $N$: a known design on $U_N$, an exposure mapping, and fixed potential outcomes satisfying Conditions 1 and 2; two distinct exposures $d_k, d_l$ with $0 < \pi_i(d) < 1$ for every $i \in U_N$ and $d \in \{d_k, d_l\}$. Write $\tau_N = \tau(d_k, d_l)$, $\widehat{\tau}_N = \widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ of expression (3), $V_N = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau}_N]$, and $\widehat{V}_N = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ of expression (11), all for the population $U_N$. [Hypotheses] (C3) Condition 3: there are constants $c_1, c_2 < \infty$, not depending on $N$, such that $|y_i(d)| \le c_1$ and $1/\pi_i(d) \le c_2$ for all $N$, all $i \in U_N$ and $d \in \{d_k, d_l\}$. (C5) Condition 5 for a genuine dependency graph: for each $N$ there is a symmetric binary $h_{ij}$, $(i, j) \in U_N \times U_N$, such that for every pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2 \subseteq U_N$ with $h_{ij} = 0$ for all $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, the random vectors $(D_i)_{i \in \Gamma_1}$ and $(D_j)_{j \in \Gamma_2}$ are independent; and there is a finite constant $m$, not depending on $N$, such that $\sum_{j \in U_N} h_{ij} \le m$ for all $N$ and all $i \in U_N$. (C6) Condition 6: $N V_N \to c$, where $c > 0$. (L) [Added] For every $\delta > 0$, $\Pr\{N\widehat{V}_N < N V_N - \delta\} \to 0$. [Conclusion] For every $0 < \alpha < 1$, $\liminf_{N \to \infty} \Pr\{|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [Sufficient conditions for (L), each stated by the validators] (A) $N(\widehat{V}_N - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N]) \xrightarrow{p} 0$ implies (L), because $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N] \ge V_N$ (Proposition 5.6); in particular $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) \to 0$ implies (L). (R) Under (C3) and (C5), suppose there is a constant $b > 0$, not depending on $N$, such that every positive joint exposure probability used by (11) is at least $b$: for all $N$ and all $i \ne j$ in $U_N$, each of $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_l)$ and $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ is either $0$ or at least $b$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = O(N^{-1})$, hence (A) and (L). (R') Under (C3) and (C5), let $b_N$ be the smallest positive value among $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_l)$, $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ over $i \ne j$ in $U_N$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = O((N b_N)^{-1})$, so $N b_N \to \infty$ implies (A) and (L). [What does not suffice] Conditions 3, 5 and 6 alone, even with the corrected dependency graph, do not imply the conclusion: P013-T1.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. The corrected dependency indicator is in P013-T6. $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution. In (C3) the bound on $1/\pi_i(d)$ and in (R) the bound $b$ are uniform over the whole sequence, not computed separately at each $N$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $N$: (i) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}_N] = \tau_N$ (Proposition 4.2, (4)); (ii) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{V}_N] \ge V_N$ (Proposition 5.6, P013-T15); (iii) for $\delta > 0$, $\Pr\{N\widehat{V}_N < N V_N - \delta\} \le \Pr\{|N\widehat{V}_N - \mathrm{E}[N\widehat{V}_N]| > \delta\} \le \mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N)/\delta^2$; (iv) with $Z_N = (\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N)/\sqrt{V_N}$, $c_N = N V_N > 0$ and $0 < \delta < c_N$, the interval covers whenever $N\widehat{V}_N \ge c_N - \delta$ and $|Z_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{1 - \delta/c_N}$, so $\Pr\{|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}\} \ge \Pr\{|Z_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{1 - \delta/c_N}\} - \Pr\{N\widehat{V}_N < c_N - \delta\}$; (v) [for (R)] $N^2\widehat{V}_N = \sum_{i,j} B_{ij}(D_i, D_j)$, where $B_{ij}$ collects the terms of (7), $\widehat{A_2}$ and (10) for the ordered pair $(i, j)$; $B_{ij} = 0$ unless $i = j$ or $h_{ij} = 1$, because independent exposures have $\pi_{ij} = \pi_i\pi_j > 0$; under (R), $|(\pi_{ij} - \pi_i\pi_j)/\pi_{ij} \cdot Y_iY_j/(\pi_i\pi_j)| \le (1 + 1/b)c_1^2c_2^2$ and so $|B_{ij}| \le C$ with $C$ depending only on $c_1, c_2, b$; $\mathrm{Cov}[B_{ij}, B_{kl}] = 0$ unless one of $i, j$ equals or is $h$-adjacent to one of $k, l$; the number of such quadruples with $B_{ij}$, $B_{kl}$ not identically zero is at most $4N(m+1)^3$; hence $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) \le 16C^2(m+1)^3/N$; (vi) [for (R')] for a term with positive joint probability $p$, $\mathrm{E}[\{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_s, D_j = d_t)\frac{p - \pi_i\pi_j}{p}\frac{Y_iY_j}{\pi_i\pi_j}\}^2] \le c_1^4c_2^4\,p(1 + 1/p)^2 \le 4c_1^4c_2^4/p$, so $\mathrm{E}[B_{ij}^2] \le C'/b_N$ and the same count with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $\mathrm{Var}(N\widehat{V}_N) = O((Nb_N)^{-1})$. Not a finite lemma: the central limit theorem $Z_N \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ under (C3), (C5), (C6), which the paper takes from Chen and Shao (2004), Theorem 2.7 (p. 1943) and does not prove; the summands $\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)y_i(d_k)/\pi_i(d_k) - \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_l)y_i(d_l)/\pi_i(d_l) - [y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]$ are mean zero, bounded by $2c_1c_2 + 2c_1$, and have dependency graph $h$.
canonical_claim.note: Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair after the doubt was applied): add (L); (A) is a sufficient convenience; (R) is a sufficient primitive strengthening of Condition 3; (R') is a weaker primitive rate. The derivations are in validate/P013-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, Section 9, and validate/P013-E001/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, Section 9 (which writes $M$ for a closed degree bound including self-edges; with the paper's $m$ that bound is $m + 1$ if $h_{ii} = 0$ and $m$ if $h_{ii} = 1$, so the constant in (v) may be taken with either convention). On the event $\widehat{V}_N < 0$ the interval may be given any convention: that event has vanishing probability under (L) and (C6), and the strictest convention counts it as non-coverage. The settled doubt also found that (R) holds automatically, given Condition 3, in the Bernoulli illustration of p. 1926 with a common rate and bounded degree and in the designs of Sections 9 and 10; those facts are the reason for the Moderate rating and are not part of this target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 4.1 and the replicate rule, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9); proof in Appendix A.3, p. 1938 (PDF p. 27)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements refuted: Proposition 4.1 and the rule $R \ge \log(b)/\log(1 - \pi_0(d_k)) - 1$, p. 1920 (PDF p. 9), and the last inequality of Appendix A.3, p. 1938 (PDF p. 27); all transcribed under P013-T12.] [Counterexample, from the validator] $N = 2$, $M = 2$, $\Omega = \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2)\}$, and $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = d_{z_i}$ (no interference; $K = 2$). The two units are assigned independently with $\Pr(Z_1 = 2) = 1/3$ and $\Pr(Z_2 = 2) = 2/3$, so $p_{(1,1)} = 2/9$, $p_{(1,2)} = 4/9$, $p_{(2,1)} = 1/9$, $p_{(2,2)} = 2/9$. Potential outcomes: $(y_1(d_1), y_2(d_1)) = (0, 0)$ and $(y_1(d_2), y_2(d_2)) = (2, -1)$, with $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i(d_{z_i})$ and $Y_i = y_i(d_{Z_i})$. Conditions 1 and 2 hold and $0 < \pi_i(d) < 1$ for both units and both exposures. Take the exposure $d_k = d_2$: $\pi_1(d_2) = 1/3$, $\pi_2(d_2) = 2/3$, $\pi_0(d_2) = 1/3$, $y^T(d_2) = 1$. Take $R = 1$: one simulated assignment $\mathbf{Z}'$ drawn from the same design independently of $\mathbf{Z}$, $X_i = \mathbf{I}(Z'_i = 2)$ and $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_2) = (X_i + 1)/2$. (a) Summing over the 16 pairs $(\mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{Z}')$ with their probabilities, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_2)] = 2/9$. The absolute relative bias is $|2/9 - 1|/|1| = 7/9$, which exceeds the printed bound $(1 - \pi_0(d_2))^{R+1} = (2/3)^2 = 4/9$. (b) [Replicate rule] For the relative bias target $b = 1/2$, $R = 1$ satisfies $R \ge \log(b)/\log(1 - \pi_0(d_2)) - 1$ (equivalently $(2/3)^{R+1} = 4/9 \le 1/2$), and it is the smallest nonnegative integer that does ($(2/3)^1 > 1/2$); yet the relative bias $7/9$ exceeds $b$. (c) [Zero total] In the same design with $(y_1(d_2), y_2(d_2)) = (1, -1)$: $y^T(d_2) = 0$ and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_2)] = -1/3$. The relative bias is undefined, and the last inequality of Appendix A.3 fails: $|\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_2)] - y^T(d_2)| = 1/3 > 0 = |y^T(d_2)|(1 - \pi_0(d_2))^{R+1}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [p. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k) = \frac{X_i + 1}{R + 1}$, where $X_i = \sum_{r=1}^{R} \mathbf{I}_r(f(\mathbf{z}_r, \theta_i) = d_k)$ and $r = 1, \ldots, R$ indexes the replicates; $\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\frac{Y_i}{\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)}$; $\pi_0(d_k) = \min_i\{\pi_i(d_k)\}$. [p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] The replicates are $R$ random replicate $\mathbf{z}$'s based on the randomization plan. The expectation is over the experiment's assignment and the replicates jointly. Setting and Conditions 1, 2: standing assumptions.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E003 is rated an error, Moderate. The identity $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] = \sum_i y_i(d_k) [1 - (1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}]$ of Appendix A.3 is correct and gives $2(5/9) - (8/9) = 2/9$ in (a) and $(5/9) - (8/9) = -1/3$ in (c); the validator's enumeration (exact_check.py, enumeration_nonzero.csv, enumeration_zero.csv, beside the derivation) computes both without using that identity. The unrestricted bound of P013-T4 gives $(|2| + |-1|)(4/9) = 4/3 \ge 7/9$ here. With the exact probabilities the estimator of expression (1) has expectation $y^T(d_2) = 1$ in this design: Lemma 4.1 is not affected.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected Proposition 4.1 and replicate rule. Changes from the printed statement: the bound is stated for the absolute bias with the factor $\sum_i |y_i(d_k)|$; the relative bound carries the factor $\kappa = \sum_i |y_i(d_k)| / |y^T(d_k)|$ and requires $y^T(d_k) 
e 0$; the printed bound and rule are kept for outcomes of one sign with nonzero total.] [Hypotheses] Conditions 1 and 2; an exposure $d_k$ with $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$; an integer $R \ge 1$; the replicates $\mathbf{z}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_R$ are independent draws from the design ($\Pr(\mathbf{z}_r = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$) and are independent of the experiment's assignment $\mathbf{Z}$; $X_i = \sum_{r=1}^{R} \mathbf{I}_r(f(\mathbf{z}_r, 	heta_i) = d_k)$, $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k) = (X_i + 1)/(R + 1)$, $\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i/\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ and $\pi_0(d_k) = \min_i\{\pi_i(d_k)\}$. The potential outcomes $y_i(d_k)$ are arbitrary real numbers except where a sign condition is stated. [Statement] (a) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)[1 - (1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}] = y^T(d_k) - \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)(1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}$. (b) $|\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] - y^T(d_k)| \le (1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} |y_i(d_k)|$. (c) If $y^T(d_k) 
e 0$, then $\left| rac{\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] - y^T(d_k)}{y^T(d_k)}ight| \le \kappa\,(1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}$, where $\kappa = \sum_{i=1}^{N} |y_i(d_k)| / |y^T(d_k)| \ge 1$. (d) If the $y_i(d_k)$ have a common sign ($y_i(d_k) \ge 0$ for all $i$, or $y_i(d_k) \le 0$ for all $i$) and $y^T(d_k) 
e 0$, then $\kappa = 1$ and the printed bound holds: $\left| rac{\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] - y^T(d_k)}{y^T(d_k)}ight| \le (1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}$. (e) [Replicate rule] Let $b > 0$ and $y^T(d_k) 
e 0$. If $R \ge \log(b/\kappa)/\log(1 - \pi_0(d_k)) - 1$, then the absolute relative bias in (c) is at most $b$. For common-sign outcomes with nonzero total this is the printed rule $R \ge \log(b)/\log(1 - \pi_0(d_k)) - 1$. (f) [The printed numerical example is unchanged] For $b = 0.005$ and $\pi_0(d_k) = 0.0005$, $(1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1} \le b$ holds for $R = 10{,}593$ and fails for $R = 10{,}592$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P013-T3. [Appendix A.3, p. 1938 (PDF p. 27), the identities that remain correct] $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{y^T_{HT,R}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)\pi_i(d_k)\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R+1}{X_i+1}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)[1 - (1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}] = y^T(d_k) - \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)(1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(R, \pi)$ with $0 < \pi \le 1$: $\pi\,\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R+1}{X+1}\right] = \sum_{x=0}^{R}\binom{R+1}{x+1}\pi^{x+1}(1-\pi)^{R-x} = 1 - (1-\pi)^{R+1}$, using $\frac{R+1}{x+1}\binom{R}{x} = \binom{R+1}{x+1}$. With $q_i = (1 - \pi_i(d_k))^{R+1}$ and $q_0 = (1 - \pi_0(d_k))^{R+1}$: $0 \le q_i \le q_0$ and $|\sum_i y_i(d_k)q_i| \le \sum_i |y_i(d_k)|q_i \le q_0\sum_i |y_i(d_k)|$.
canonical_claim.note:
Sol's smallest repair: for $y^T(d_k) \ne 0$ multiply the printed right-hand side by $\sum_i |y_i(d_k)|/|y^T(d_k)|$; state the absolute version for all totals, including zero; in the replicate rule replace $b$ by $b/\kappa$; alternatively restrict the proposition and rule to common-sign outcomes with nonzero total. Common sign is sufficient, not necessary: if all $\pi_i(d_k)$ are equal the bias is exactly $-y^T(d_k)q_0$ and the printed bound holds for mixed signs. The validator also shows that no finite $R$ depending only on $\pi_0$ and $b$ guarantees the relative target over all signed nonzero totals with unequal probabilities (derivation.md, Section 4). The independence of the replicates from each other and from $\mathbf{Z}$ is the reading under which Appendix A.3 computes $\mathrm{E}[(R+1)/(X_i+1)]$; the proof of Proposition 3.1 says “without replacement” (P013-E010, a clarity note; see P013-T20).

Accepted review: the duplicate-rejecting Bernoulli defect belongs to the staged later interference package snapshot (version 0.1.0, commit c3fc7b3), whose DESCRIPTION credits Stephanie Zonszein, Cyrus Samii and Peter Aronow. This author list does not identify who introduced the defect. Use of that snapshot or its replication script for the original published calculations is not established, and no published-table error follows from the package check. The mathematical results here use independent whole-design replicate draws; they do not validate duplicate rejection under a nonuniform design. Appendix A.1's original without-replacement wording is the separate P013-E010 clarity note, not another count of the later implementation defect. The signed-outcome correction and independent-draw repair are unchanged.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition of the dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ and Condition 5, as printed, with the claim that Condition 5 subsumes Condition 4
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statements refuted: the definition of $h_{ij}$ and Condition 5, p. 1925 (PDF p. 14), transcribed in the standing assumptions, together with p. 1926 (PDF p. 15):] Condition 5 is equivalent to assuming that dependencies across exposures can be represented by a dependency graph such that the maximal degree of each unit tends to be limited relative to $N$. [...] Note that Condition 5 subsumes Condition 4, as $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = O(N)$ when Condition 5 holds. [Counterexample, from the validator] (a) [The printed definition is vacuous for the identity indicator.] For any $N \ge 1$ let $h_{ij} = 1$ if $i = j$ and $h_{ij} = 0$ otherwise. For disjoint $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2 \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$, the printed antecedent (“there exists no pair $(i, j)$ with $h_{ij} = 1$ and either (i), (ii), (iii) or (iv)”) holds if and only if $\Gamma_1 = \Gamma_2 = \emptyset$: if $i \in \Gamma_1$ the pair $(i, i)$ satisfies clause (i), since $i 
otin \Gamma_2$; if $i \in \Gamma_2$ the pair $(i, i)$ satisfies clause (iii), since $i 
otin \Gamma_1$. Hence this $h$ satisfies the printed definition for every joint distribution of $(D_1, \ldots, D_N)$, and $\sum_j h_{ij} = 1$ for every $i$. (b) [The same without self-loops.] For $N = 3q$ let $h_{ij} = 1$ exactly when $i 
e j$ lie in the same block of the partition $\{1, 2, 3\}, \{4, 5, 6\}, \ldots$. This $h$ is symmetric with zero diagonal and every row sum equals 2, and again the printed antecedent holds only for $\Gamma_1 = \Gamma_2 = \emptyset$, so $h$ satisfies the printed definition for every joint distribution of the exposures. (c) [Condition 5 as printed holds and Condition 4 fails.] Let $N \ge 2$, binary treatment with $\Omega = \{(0, \ldots, 0), (1, \ldots, 1)\}$, each assignment having probability $1/2$, and $D_i = Z_i$, so that all units share one fair Bernoulli exposure and $\pi_i(1) = \pi_i(0) = 1/2$. For all $i, j$, $\Pr(D_i = 1, D_j = 1) = 1/2 
e 1/4 = \Pr(D_i = 1)\Pr(D_j = 1)$, so no two exposures are independent, every $g_{ij}$ must equal 1, and $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = N^2$, which is neither $O(N)$ nor $o(N^2)$. Yet Condition 5 as printed holds with $m = 1$ (the $h$ of (a)), and with $m = 2$ when $3$ divides $N$ (the $h$ of (b)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed definition of $h_{ij}$, Conditions 4 and 5 and the definition of $g_{ij}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions (p. 1925, PDF p. 14). The paper does not say whether $h_{ii}$ is 0 or 1, nor that $h$ is symmetric; (a) uses $h_{ii} = 1$ and (b) uses $h_{ii} = 0$.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E002 is rated an error, Minor: four wrong membership symbols, with the intended dependency graph named on the next page. The statements in (a)–(c) hold for each $N$ exactly; the failure of $O(N)$ and $o(N^2)$ is read along the sequence. The validator adds a second example (derivation.md, Section 3), not required of this target: for $N = 36r^2$, a design that chooses the number treated $S$ from $\{18r^2 - 9r, 18r^2, 18r^2 + 9r\}$ with probabilities $1/18, 8/9, 1/18$ and then a uniform assignment with $S$ ones, with $D_i = Z_i$, $y_i(1) = 1$, $y_i(0) = 0$, satisfies Conditions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 as printed (the $h$ of (b), $m = 2$) and 6 ($N\,\mathrm{Var} = 1$), while $(\widehat{\tau_{HT}} - \tau)/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}}$ takes the values $-3, 0, 3$ with probabilities $1/18, 8/9, 1/18$ for every $r$ and the interval of Proposition 6.2 with critical value 2 has coverage exactly $8/9$ for every $r \ge 5$. The corrected definition (P013-T6) excludes all of these examples.
